title: Why 200 versions of a file take almost no space
summary: Git stores whole snapshots, yet a repository with a thousand versions of a file is tiny. Packfiles and delta compression are the reason — open one and read the deltas.
mental_model: The data model is snapshots; the storage is deltas. When git packs, it finds objects that resemble each other and stores most of them as a small diff against a chosen base. Nothing about the model changes — only the bytes on disk.

steps.title: Create many versions of one large-ish file
steps.why: Forty commits, each changing one line of a 400-line file. Stored naively that is forty near-identical copies — a good demonstration of what packing is for.

actions.run: sh -c 'for i in $(seq 1 40); do { echo "# generated file, revision $i"; for j in $(seq 1 400); do echo "CONSTANT_$j = $j"; done; } > config.py; git add config.py; git commit -q -m "Regenerate config, revision $i"; done'

steps.expect: Around 120 loose objects and a size-on-disk of a few hundred kilobytes.

steps.title: Measure the naive cost
steps.why: Loose objects are zlib-compressed individually, with no knowledge of each other. Forty near-identical files compress to forty similar blobs — no sharing at all.
steps.expect: One object file per blob, tree and commit.

steps.title: Pack them
steps.why: `repack -ad` builds a single optimal packfile. Git compares objects, picks bases, and stores the rest as deltas — the size drop is often an order of magnitude.
steps.expect: Loose count near zero, one .pack and one .idx file, size-pack far smaller than before.

steps.title: Read inside the packfile
steps.why: `verify-pack -v` lists every object with its type, size, packed size and delta depth. Objects with a base sha at the end of the line are stored as deltas against that object.
steps.expect: Blobs listed with sizes and chain depths.

steps.title: See the delta chains
steps.why: Most of those forty config blobs are stored as small deltas against one full copy. The fifth column is the packed size — compare it with the object's real size in the third.
steps.expect: A handful of full-size objects, and many stored in a fraction of their real size.

steps.title: Prove nothing was lost
steps.why: The data model is unchanged: every blob still reads back byte for byte. Delta storage is invisible above the object layer, which is why nothing else in git has to know about it.
steps.expect: The full 401-line file, reconstructed from a delta chain on demand.

verify.label: an old version reads back complete from the pack

steps.title: The index file beside the pack
steps.why: A `.pack` holds the objects; the `.idx` maps each sha to an offset within it. Without the index, finding one object would mean scanning the whole pack — with it, lookup is a binary search.
steps.expect: A pack and an idx of very different sizes.

steps.title: What controls the trade-off
steps.why: `pack.depth` caps how long a delta chain may be — longer chains are smaller on disk but slower to read. `pack.window` controls how many candidate bases git considers. Both are worth knowing exist and rarely worth changing.
commands: sh -c 'git config pack.depth 50 && git config pack.window 250 && git config --get-regexp pack | cat'

verify.label: the delta chain depth is configured
the repository's objects live in a packfile
old versions still read back in full from delta chains

pitfalls: Packing is storage, not the data model. Git still conceptually stores snapshots; anyone who tells you git stores diffs is describing the pack format.
A repository full of large binaries packs badly — binaries rarely delta well against each other. That is the case where LFS earns its keep.
`git gc --aggressive` recomputes deltas from scratch. It is slow, occasionally worth it after importing a repository, and pointless as a routine.
Never delete a `.pack` without its `.idx`, or the other way round. They are a pair.
